journal_name: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems

abstracts.abstract: We present a foundational reconceptualization of effect handling in functional programming languages through a novel coeffect-aware type system that fundamentally shifts how we reason about resource consumption and contextual requirements. Traditional effect systems track what computations do, yet ignore essential questions about what computations require from their execution environment. Our approach introduces annotated coeffect types that precisely characterize resource dependencies, environmental constraints, and implicit data flows that propagate through program execution. We formalize this framework through a λ-calculus extension with coeffect signatures and develop a sound and complete type inference algorithm based on constraint propagation over coeffect lattices. The key theoretical contribution lies in establishing a duality between effects (what computations produce) and coeffects (what computations consume), enabling a symmetric treatment of both dimensions within a unified type theory. We prove that well-typed programs satisfy a novel property of contextual safety: programs cannot access resources or environmental features beyond their declared coeffect signatures. This work opens new theoretical directions for programming language design by demonstrating that incorporating resource consumption into the core type system enables novel program verification techniques impossible within traditional effect-based frameworks. Our results have immediate implications for program analysis, security-critical code verification, and the design of resource-aware programming languages.

This paper presents significant theoretical advances in flow-sensitive program analysis through a novel abstract interpretation framework that dramatically improves precision and efficiency over existing approaches. While prior work on flow-sensitive analysis has struggled to balance computational tractability with analysis precision, particularly for programs with complex aliasing and dynamic memory behavior, our approach introduces a new form of indexed environment semantics that maintains precisely tracked heap abstractions without sacrificing scalability. We develop a complete formal characterization of our analysis framework, proving that it achieves significantly stronger soundness guarantees than traditional flow-sensitive pointer analyses while maintaining polynomial-time complexity for a substantially larger class of programs. Our theoretical contributions include novel theorems establishing the relationship between environment indexing depth and analysis precision, providing actionable guidelines for practitioners seeking to configure analysis tools for specific verification tasks. We further demonstrate that our framework subsumes several existing analysis techniques as special cases, unifying previously disparate approaches under a common theoretical foundation. Experimental validation on standard benchmarks confirms theoretical predictions, showing improvements of up to 40% in detection of memory safety violations compared to state-of-the-art analyses while reducing analysis time by an order of magnitude for large-scale codebases.

We introduce SynthLang, a groundbreaking domain-specific language and synthesis engine that represents a paradigm shift in program synthesis by treating specification and implementation as interchangeable semantic representations within a unified framework. Unlike existing synthesis systems that require users to provide formal specifications separate from executable code, SynthLang enables programmers to write specifications that are simultaneously executable and verifiable, with bidirectional transformation between concrete programs and abstract requirements. The system architecture centers on a novel semantic anchoring mechanism that maintains logical equivalence between specification expressions and their executable counterparts throughout the development process. We present a complete implementation including a type-safe compiler targeting multiple backend platforms, an interactive synthesis debugger supporting bidirectional stepping between specification and implementation views, and a verification engine that proves equivalence properties in real-time during development. The language design incorporates concepts from dependent type theory while remaining accessible to programmers without formal methods expertise. Our implementation demonstrates practical applicability through case studies in cryptographic protocol development, where SynthLang's ability to automatically extract efficient implementations from high-level security specifications eliminates an entire class of implementation vulnerabilities. The system operates at a level of abstraction fundamentally different from existing synthesis tools, enabling users to reason about what programs should accomplish while the system automatically manages the complex relationships between specification and implementation.

We present RustVerify 2.0, a substantially enhanced program verification system for Rust that achieves unprecedented precision and usability in proving memory safety and concurrency properties. Building on lessons from first-generation Rust verification tools, our system introduces a novel intermediate verification language specifically designed for Rust's ownership and borrowing semantics, combined with an improved SMT solver integration that leverages semantic knowledge of Rust's type system to reduce solving complexity. The architecture features a modular verification condition generation approach that maintains precise ownership information throughout the verification process, eliminating soundness issues present in prior tools that required over-approximation of reference semantics. We introduce several engineering contributions including incremental verification supporting fast re-verification during development, a visual counterexample exploration interface, and automated lemma synthesis for common proof patterns in ownership reasoning. The system has been evaluated on a comprehensive benchmark suite comprising 50,000 lines of real-world Rust code, demonstrating a 73% reduction in verification time compared to existing approaches while increasing the proportion of successfully verified safety properties from 64% to 91%. RustVerify 2.0 is publicly available and has been adopted by several industrial teams for safety-critical Rust development, validating its practical utility beyond academic benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that careful co-design of verification theory and implementation engineering can achieve substantial improvements in both scalability and applicability of program verification technology.
